nutshell: Text-to-image person ReID (TIReID) methods implicitly assume training image-text pairs are correctly aligned, but real datasets inevitably contain 'noisy correspondence' (NC) - mismatched or false-positive pairs from annotation error or ambiguous images. RDE addresses this with a Confident Consensus Division (CCD) module that uses two differently-grained embedding branches to jointly identify clean vs. noisy training pairs, plus a Triplet Alignment Loss (TAL) that relaxes the standard hardest-negative triplet loss into a stable upper bound, together preventing the model collapse that noisy pairs otherwise cause.
contributions: Identifies and names noisy correspondence (NC) as a distinct problem in TIReID specifically (as opposed to noisy class labels or NC in other cross-modal tasks), framing it as false-positive image-text pairs rather than mislabeled classes.

Confident Consensus Division (CCD): fits a per-sample GMM over training loss separately for a coarse global embedding (BGE) and a fine-grained token-selection embedding (TSE), then takes the intersection of both branches' clean/noisy decisions as a confident consensus set - pairs where the two views disagree are treated as uncertain rather than trusted outright, which is more conservative than a single-branch noise-division approach.

Triplet Alignment Loss (TAL): a provable upper bound (Lemma 1) on the standard Triplet Ranking Loss that replaces optimization against only the single hardest negative with a temperature-controlled log-sum-exp over all negatives - shown via gradient analysis and empirical similarity-distribution plots (Fig. 3) to prevent the total representational collapse that the standard loss exhibits under noise (63.35% vs. 3.64% Rank-1 at 50% noise).

State-of-the-art results on CUHK-PEDES, ICFG-PEDES, and RSTPReid, both under synthetic noise (20%/50% randomly shuffled captions) and on the original clean datasets, and demonstrates near-zero gap between 'best-checkpoint' and 'last-epoch' performance (Table 1), indicating resistance to the overfitting-to-noise pattern that baseline methods show.
deficiencies: The noise injected for evaluation is purely synthetic - randomly shuffling text descriptions to create fully mismatched pairs - rather than the kind of real annotation noise the paper's own motivating example (Figure 1) shows, where a caption is only partially wrong (a few incorrect attributes) rather than describing a completely different scene. Randomly shuffled pairs are near-zero semantic overlap and likely much easier to detect via loss than the subtle partial mismatches that actually occur in datasets like RSTPReid; the method is never validated against naturally-occurring noise at a known rate.

The ablation in Table 2 shows CCD contributes comparatively little on its own: removing it (#5, TAL-only) only drops Rank-1 from 71.33 to 70.70 (-0.63), far less than removing TSE (#6, -2.26) or removing BGE entirely (#7, -8.22) - the paper's title and framing center on the noise-correction mechanism (CCD), but the ablation suggests the dual-embedding architecture and TAL loss are doing most of the actual work.

The 'uncertain' pairs identified by CCD (where the two embedding branches disagree) are handled by randomly assigning them a 0/1 correspondence label (Eq. 4) rather than being discarded, down-weighted, or handled with any more principled mechanism - this design choice isn't isolated or justified against simpler alternatives (e.g. simply excluding uncertain pairs from that epoch's loss) anywhere in the ablation.

The GMM clean/noisy division threshold (delta=0.5) and the reliance on a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model over per-sample loss are used without any sensitivity analysis or discussion of failure modes - all reported experiments cap noise at 50%, and there's no exploration of how the consensus-division mechanism behaves as true noise rates approach the point where a bimodal GMM fit becomes unreliable.
notable: The Triplet Alignment Loss is explicitly presented as a temperature-controlled interpolation between two known losses - it collapses toward the standard hardest-negative Triplet Ranking Loss as tau to 0 and toward the more stable (but less discriminative) sum-over-all-negatives variant (TRL-S) as tau grows - with Lemma 1 formally proving TAL upper-bounds TRL. This 'soft hardest-negative via log-sum-exp temperature' pattern is a general, reusable trick for any metric-learning triplet loss beyond ReID, not specific to the noisy-correspondence setting. Also notable: the best-vs-last-checkpoint comparison in Table 1 is arguably stronger evidence of robustness than the headline SOTA numbers - baselines like SSAN and IVT show real accuracy drops between best and last checkpoint under 50% noise (e.g. SSAN Rank-1 13.43 to 11.31), while RDE's best/last gap is negligible (71.33 vs. 71.25), directly demonstrating resistance to noise-overfitting rather than just higher peak accuracy.
